title: What Are REO Properties and How to Buy Them: A Complete Investor's Guide
excerpt: REO properties are bank-owned homes that survived foreclosure without selling at auction — and they can be goldmines for savvy investors who know where to look. This guide breaks down exactly what REO properties are, how they work, and the step-by-step process to buy one at a discount.
author: AIWholesail Team
metaDescription: Learn what REO properties are and how to buy them with this step-by-step guide for real estate investors, wholesalers, and flippers.

sections.content: If you've spent any time studying real estate investing, you've probably heard the term REO thrown around. But what are REO properties exactly, and how do you actually buy one? REO stands for Real Estate Owned — it's the industry term for properties that a bank or lender has taken back after a failed foreclosure auction. These homes didn't sell at the courthouse steps, so the lender is now stuck owning them. That creates an opportunity for investors. Banks are not in the business of managing real estate, and they're often motivated to sell these properties quickly, sometimes well below market value. REO deals fit naturally into any strategy focused on finding motivated sellers — in fact, our [How to Find Motivated Sellers: Complete Guide](aiwholesail.com/guides/finding-motivated-sellers) covers REOs alongside other powerful lead sources every serious investor should know.
How a Property Becomes REO

Understanding the path a property takes to become REO helps you know exactly when and where to step in. Here's the typical timeline. A homeowner stops making mortgage payments, usually for 90 to 120 days. The lender files a Notice of Default, kicking off the formal foreclosure process. The property is then listed at a public foreclosure auction where the starting bid is usually the amount owed on the loan, including fees. If no one bids above that amount — which happens more often than you'd think, especially when the loan balance is higher than the home's current value — the lender takes the property back. At that point, it becomes REO. The lender clears the title, removes any occupants, and lists it for sale, usually through a traditional real estate agent or a specialized REO asset management company.
Why REO Properties Appeal to Real Estate Investors

The biggest draw is price. Banks don't want to carry real estate on their books. It costs them money in maintenance, insurance, property taxes, and regulatory capital requirements. A lender sitting on 200 REO properties has a strong incentive to sell fast and move on. That motivation translates to below-market pricing, flexible negotiation, and sometimes seller-paid closing costs. REO properties also come with cleared titles in most cases, unlike properties bought at auction where you might inherit liens and back taxes. You also typically get the right to inspect the property before closing — a major advantage over courthouse-step buying. If you're already exploring [how to find distressed properties before they hit MLS](aiwholesail.com/blog/find-distressed-properties-before-mls), REO inventory is one of the most reliable and consistently available distressed property sources in any market cycle.

Banks are motivated sellers by nature. They're holding an asset they never wanted and can't profit from. That's the foundation of every good REO deal. — Common wisdom among experienced real estate investors
How to Find REO Properties

There are several reliable channels for finding REO listings. The most straightforward is the MLS, where bank-owned homes are often labeled as REO or bank-owned in the listing remarks. Larger banks like Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and Chase have dedicated REO portals on their websites. Government-backed loan programs also generate their own REO inventory — HUD homes come from FHA-backed loans, Fannie Mae lists properties on HomePath.com, and Freddie Mac uses HomeSteps.com. For investors who want to go deeper, county courthouse records and tax assessor databases show properties in various stages of default, letting you reach out before a property even makes it to an REO list. Pair that with other off-market lead strategies — like [absentee owner lists](aiwholesail.com/blog/absentee-owner-list-deals) and [inherited property leads](aiwholesail.com/blog/inherited-property-leads) — and you build a robust pipeline that doesn't depend on competition from other buyers.

Pro Tip: Build a direct relationship with REO asset managers at local and regional banks. These are the people who decide which investors get first looks at new inventory. A quick phone call or LinkedIn message introducing yourself as a cash buyer can get you deals before they ever hit a listing portal.
Step-by-Step: How to Buy an REO Property
Step 1 — Get Your Financing Ready

Banks selling REO properties strongly prefer buyers who can close quickly and cleanly. If you're paying cash, have your proof of funds ready to attach to every offer. If you're using financing, get a pre-approval letter from your lender before you start making offers. Conventional loans, hard money loans, and portfolio loans all work for REO purchases, but cash offers consistently win in competitive situations.
Step 2 — Run Your Numbers Before You Offer

This is the step most beginners skip, and it kills deals or creates losses. You need to know the after-repair value (ARV), estimated repair costs, and your target profit before submitting any offer. Use the free [Wholesale Deal Calculator at aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator](aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to quickly model your deal and make sure the numbers work before you're emotionally invested. A common formula for flippers is the 70% rule: offer no more than 70% of ARV minus repair costs. So if a home has an ARV of $250,000 and needs $40,000 in repairs, your maximum offer is ($250,000 x 0.70) - $40,000 = $135,000.
Step 3 — Submit a Clean, Competitive Offer

REO offers go through an asset manager, not a motivated homeowner. Banks respond to clean contracts with minimal contingencies, large earnest money deposits (typically 1% to 3% of the purchase price), and fast close timelines — usually 15 to 30 days. Attach your proof of funds or pre-approval letter, keep the contingencies tight, and be prepared to negotiate. Banks often counter at or near list price at first. Don't take the first counter personally. Come back with data — comparable sales, repair estimates, and your projected timeline — and make your case professionally.
Step 4 — Complete Your Due Diligence

Once you're under contract, move fast. Order a full home inspection immediately. REO properties are sold as-is, meaning the bank will not make repairs, but your inspection still tells you exactly what you're getting into. Order a title search to confirm the bank has cleared all liens. If the property has been vacant for a long time, pay special attention to HVAC systems, plumbing, roof condition, and any signs of water intrusion or mold. Get contractor bids during your inspection period so you're not estimating repairs — you're working with real numbers.
Step 5 — Close and Execute Your Strategy

Once due diligence checks out, move toward closing. REO closings are largely standard, though banks often use their own addenda and closing documents. Review everything carefully, especially clauses around as-is condition and any warranties (usually none). Once you close, execute your investment strategy — whether that's a flip, a wholesale assignment, a rental conversion, or a BRRRR play. If you're interested in building long-term wealth through rentals, check out our guide on [passive real estate investing](aiwholesail.com/guides/passive-real-estate-investing) for a framework that makes buy-and-hold REO properties cash flow effectively.
Active REO Markets Worth Watching

REO inventory tends to concentrate in markets with high foreclosure activity, population growth, and strong investor demand. Right now, [Atlanta, GA](aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas, TX](aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix, AZ](aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) all offer strong REO pipelines with solid ARVs and active buyer pools — ideal conditions for flipping or wholesaling bank-owned properties. Each market has its own rhythm, so understanding local foreclosure laws, redemption periods, and average days on market for REO listings is essential before you dive in.
Common Mistakes to Avoid With REO Properties

items: Skipping the inspection because the bank says it's as-is — always inspect, even if you can't require repairs
Underestimating repair costs on properties that have been vacant for 12+ months
Offering without a proof of funds letter — banks will ignore unverified offers
Assuming every REO is a great deal — run the numbers on every single property
Missing the counteroffer deadline — banks move on quickly and relist without warning
Not accounting for carrying costs during a longer renovation period
Forgetting to check for HOA dues, special assessments, or municipal liens that survived foreclosure
